content:
Hydrotherapy — exercising in warm water (33-36°C) — is one of the most effective treatments for arthritis. The warmth relaxes muscles and eases pain, while the water's buoyancy supports your body weight, reducing stress on joints.

Quick answer: Hydrotherapy is exercising in warm water, typically between 33-36°C, to relieve arthritis symptoms. The warmth relaxes muscles and eases pain, while water's buoyancy supports body weight, reducing joint stress. Benefits include pain relief, reduced stiffness, muscle strengthening, and improved balance. Access hydrotherapy through NHS physiotherapy referrals or community leisure centres offering warm water sessions.

Benefits of Hydrotherapy for Arthritis

  • Pain relief — warm water raises body temperature, increasing blood flow and releasing endorphins
  • Reduced stiffness — heat and gentle movement improve joint mobility
  • Muscle strengthening — water provides natural resistance without joint impact
  • Improved balance — water supports you, making balance exercises safer
  • Psychological benefits — warm water promotes relaxation and stress relief

How to Access Hydrotherapy in the UK

NHS Hydrotherapy

Many NHS trusts offer hydrotherapy through physiotherapy departments:

  1. Ask your GP for a referral to NHS physiotherapy
  2. Request hydrotherapy specifically — not all physiotherapy includes pool sessions
  3. Typical NHS course: 6-8 sessions with a physiotherapist in the pool
  4. Waiting times vary by area — typically 6-12 weeks

Community Hydrotherapy

  • Many leisure centres offer warm water sessions or arthritis-friendly swim times
  • Search "warm water swimming" or "hydrotherapy" on your local council website
  • Some centres offer discounted rates for people with health conditions

What to Expect

  • Water temperature is typically 33-36°C (warmer than a normal pool at 27-29°C)
  • Sessions usually last 30-45 minutes
  • A physiotherapist guides you through exercises in the water
  • You don't need to be a swimmer — exercises are done standing or with floats
  • Wear a comfortable swimsuit; the pool has handrails and steps for easy access

Finding Pools Near You

  • Ask your GP or physiotherapist for local recommendations
  • Check your local council's leisure services website
  • Contact local arthritis support groups — they often know the best facilities
  • Some private physiotherapy clinics have on-site hydrotherapy pools

Hydrotherapy may not be suitable if you have certain heart conditions, skin infections, or open wounds. Discuss with your GP before starting.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Supplements versus meals

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

Quick questions about Hydrotherapy Pools Near Guide

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
